1.note: The edition points חָבֵר (ḥaver, "a companion"), not חֶבֶר (Ḥever). The teller names him Ḥever the Kenite at the end of the gate, so the word is read as his name; it can also mean "I found a companion there".

2.note: Literally "to my footstool" (הֲדוֹם). The word is chosen for the rhyme with עִמִּי; read as "my dwelling".

3.note: Literally "good bearing". It seems to render the Arabic ṣabr jamīl, "beautiful patience" (in grief).

4.he: כִּי תְהִלּוֹתַי הָיוּ חוֹבָה. וְקִינוֹתַי נְדָבָה
4.note: The answer seems to mean that the praises were owed to a living patron who paid for them, and so had to be his best work; the laments were a free gift to a dead man, from whom nothing more could come.

5.note: בְּדָלְחֵי is obscure. "Beads" is a guess from the context (רָבִיד, "necklace", Gen 41:42); the image is of necklace beads as dewdrops on the tree.

6.note: Og is the giant of Deut 3:11. Gog (Ezek 38-39) is not short in any tradition; he is here for the rhyme with Og.

7.note: That is, the grave itself: he would rather his daughters died than married.

8.note: אֲשִׁישָׁה is a raisin cake in the Bible (2 Sam 6:19, Hos 3:1); medieval readers often took it as a flask of wine, which fits a drinker here. The right and left hands may echo Song 2:5-6.

9.note: The barb plays on "closing the breaches": the other man's father "closed" them only by running away through them, while the speaker's father held them with his spear. The exact sense of the joke is uncertain.
